title: More Bhagats ahead
hookLine: Namdev, Ravidas, Dhanna, Sain and others wait for year three

lines: THE END OF A DINNER PARTY.
cards: The last guests are leaving a long dinner, and across the room there's a whole table of people nobody got to meet. Someone's laughing, someone's telling a story, and the thought is: next time.
For twelve days this path has sat with two voices, Kabir and Farid. But the Guru's book has a much bigger table. Today, a first glimpse of the others.

teach.b: Walk past that table and hear the names. Namdev, from Maharashtra, a calico printer; stories say he sang so lovingly that a temple turned toward him.
Ravidas of Benares, a leatherworker from a caste many refused to touch; he sang of Begampura, a city without sorrow, where no one is second-class. Dhanna, a farmer from Rajasthan.
Sain, a barber who, it's said, served at a king's court. Pipa, a king who, tradition says, gave up his throne to become a devotee.
Trilochan, Beni, Jaidev, Bhikhan, Sadhna, Ramanand, Parmanand, Surdas. Hindus and Muslims, Brahmins and people shut out of temples, across several centuries and much of India.
You'll meet them properly later on the path, in year three.

teach.h: TWELVE DAYS WITH KABIR AND FARID.
teach.b: For now, look back at twelve days with just two of them. Kabir the weaver, whose loom was a prayer. One light made all.
The warrior who fights for the helpless. The death that delights. Short, sharp saloks.
Farid of Pakpattan, speaking in his own Punjabi. Don't strike back. The Creator in creation.
Spare the eyes. And the Gurus answering, gently, across the centuries.

teach.h: ONE GOD, THE NAME, NO WALLS.
teach.b: What they share is what the Gurus heard in them: one God, the Name, love over ritual, and no patience for the walls people build between each other.
That's why their words sit in the Guru's book, and why the book still has more voices ahead.

how: The hymns of all the Bhagats are read and sung in Sikh worship alongside the Gurus', and communities such as the followers of Ravidas and Namdev especially cherish their hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib.

games.q: you're choosing whose hymns belong in the Guru's book. what did the Gurus look for?
o: one God, the Name, love over ritual, and no walls between people.
games.why: printer, leatherworker, farmer, barber, king: the Gurus kept voices that sang what they sang.

practice: Pick one name you heard, Namdev, Ravidas, Dhanna, Sain, Pipa, any one, and say it aloud, softly, once. Think of what they were: a printer, a leatherworker, a farmer, a barber, a king.
Let that name stand for everyone whose work the world overlooks, and whose voice was still kept.
